newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels prepare for fresh crisis talks Monday.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels prepare for fresh crisis talks Monday.

text.p: A Peruvian doctor said 72 men held captive by Marxist rebels were mostly in good shape as the government and guerrillas prepared on Sunday for fresh talks to end the 68-day Lima hostage siege.

"There is no one who is grave, who requires urgent attention outside the site and they are all in good condition, generally speaking," doctor Victor Lucero Rondon, himself a former hostage, told local television.

Police, meanwhile, broadened their musical repertoire on Sunday in a bid to soothe the savage breast of Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels ahead of fresh talks on Monday to end the crisis at the Japanese ambassador's home.

From speakers placed outside the mansion in the normally quiet San Isidro district, police special forces blared tunes ranging from opera and Mexican rancheras to easy listening and romantic rock ballads.

Since heavily armed rebels stormed the building on Dec. 17, police have used music as a psychological weapon against the MRTA guerrillas as well as to alleviate boredom around the diplomatic compound in the longest hostage siege in Latin America's history.
Their tastes have evolved from military marches in the siege's early days to traditional guitar-based "criollo" waltzs and, more recently, to romantic rock ballads and classical music.

On Sunday, hostages, rebels, neighbours and the news media were treated to Beethoven and Vivaldi concertos, an opera sung by Placido Domingo, the "Theme from Love Story" and "Take My Breath Away" from the Hollywood movie Top Gun.

The musical potpourri masked the seriousness of the human drama at play as the Peruvian government and the MRTA prepared to meet on Monday for the fifth time in two weeks in a bid to set an agenda for formal negotiations to end the ordeal.
President Alberto Fujimori said on Saturday that preliminary negotiations progressed some in the latest round of talks on Thursday but that a peaceful solution to the crisis was likely to take weeks.
"We cannot predict how many more weeks these discussions will take," he said during a tour of a poor Lima district with Japan's talks observer Terusuke Terada.
Fujimori also said he hoped rebel chief Nestor cerpa Cartolini would take part again in Monday's talks, which were slated to begin at 11 a.m. (1600 GMT).
The fact Cerpa attended the fourth round of talks was a "small advance" in the search for a peaceful solution to the crisis, he said.
"This was a great advantage because there was no need to use the red phone," he said, referring to a phone link between the residence and the talks site in a safe house across the street.
In the first three meetings, the MRTA was represented by Cerpa's deputy Rolly Rojas, alias "El Arabe" (The Arab), who used the phone to consult his chief.

Thursday's meeting was seen as a breakthrough because it was the first time Cerpa left the besieged residence since he and his band of well-armed guerrillas stormed the building during a cocktail party to celebrate the Japanese emperor's birthday.

The rebels were demanding freedom for 400 jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages' lives. The government has flatly rejected the demand but was willing to allow the hostage-takers to seek asylum abroad.

Troops manning the roadblock across a street leading to the siege site barred the way on Saturday to two white-scarfed members of Argentine human rights group Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, who wanted to visit the hostages.
The Mothers, famous for their struggle against Argentina's military rulers in the 1970s, said they would return on Sunday to try again.

Rebels initially seized hundreds of guests at the resaidence but have released all but 72, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassador's and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
